title: Multiplicative-Weights Methods and Gibbs-State Preparation for Conic Portfolio Optimization: A Mathematical Framework Connecting Quantum Algorithms, Jordan Algebras, and Quantitative Finance
abstract_summary: This preprint develops a unified mathematical pathway linking conic formulations of portfolio optimization (LP, SOCP, SDP) to multiplicative-weights feasibility solvers, Jordan-algebraic exponentials, and the arrowhead matrix embedding of Lorentz cones to simplify Gibbs-state computations. It provides SOCP encodings for mean–variance, Sharpe ratio, CVaR and robust portfolio problems, derives an explicit rank‑two spectral structure that yields O(N) Gibbs-state preparation per cone, gives full MW algorithm specifications with complexity bounds, and analyzes conditioning, data‑access models, and SDP relaxations for cardinality constraints.
methodology_description: This work is a theoretical and algorithmic study that develops a mathematical and computational pipeline connecting conic formulations of portfolio optimization (LP, SOCP, SDP) to multiplicative-weights (MW) feasibility solvers and Gibbs-state representations, with particular emphasis on the Lorentz (second-order) cone. The paper (i) expresses common portfolio problems (mean–variance, Sharpe-ratio via quasi-convex bisection, CVaR, robust variants) in conic form; (ii) formulates MW and matrix-MW (Arora–Kale style) as feasibility solvers and provides full proofs of regret/iteration bounds; (iii) derives an explicit arrowhead matrix embedding of the Lorentz cone, gives its spectral decomposition via rank-two structure, and proves equivalence between the Jordan-algebra exponential and the matrix exponential; (iv) uses this structure to simplify Gibbs-state computations for SOCP blocks (rank-2 closed form) and to state per-iteration complexity improvements; (v) compares classical, quantum, and “dequantized” Gibbs-preparation approaches, specifying input models (qRAM, sample-and-query) and indicating where quantum speedups depend on access assumptions; and (vi) analyzes conditioning effects, numerical stability, and SDP relaxations for cardinality constraints. Throughout the paper the methodology is analytical: formal problem reductions, derivation of closed-form formulas, algorithm specification (pseudocode for MW-SOCP and Sharpe bisection), oracle models, complexity proofs with explicit parameter dependence, and discussion of practical preprocessing and numerical choices. No empirical experiments or datasets are used; the contribution is algorithmic theory, proofs, and complexity/resource analyses intended to support implementations.

results_summary: The preprint develops a theoretical framework connecting conic portfolio optimization (LP/SOCP/SDP) with multiplicative-weights feasibility solvers and explicit algebraic structure of Lorentz cones. Key mathematical contributions are an arrowhead PSD embedding of Lorentz-cone elements, closed-form Jordan-algebra exponentials, and rank-2 spectral formulas that simplify Gibbs-state (normalized matrix exponential) computation for SOCP blocks. Leveraging these structural simplifications, the authors present MW-based SOCP feasibility algorithms with iteration complexity O(R^2 log N / ε^2) and per-iteration cost linear in the problem dimension under an oracle model. The paper discusses classical, quantum, and quantum-inspired Gibbs-preparation methods, claims theoretical quantum complexity improvements under strong data-access assumptions, analyzes conditioning issues relevant to finance data, and outlines SDP relaxations for cardinality constraints. Results are presented as theoretical derivations and algorithmic complexity bounds rather than empirical benchmarks.
performance_claims: T = O(R^2 log N / ε^2) iterations for MW-based SDP/SOCP feasibility (Theorem-level complexity).
Per-iteration Gibbs-state computation cost for an SOCP using arrowhead/rank-2 structure: O(sum_j d_j) = O(N) (Corollary 5.9 / algorithmic claim).
Naive SDP embedding would require O(N^3) work for general matrix exponentials (comparative claim).
Quantum MW algorithms (informal) claimed complexity scaling as e^{O}(√r · poly(m, R, 1/ε)) under coherent query access (Section 7.3, informal statement).
Sharpe-ratio maximization reduced to O(log(τ_max/ε)) SOCP feasibility solves via bisection (standard bisection complexity statement).
Gibbs-state spectral simplification: each Lorentz-block Gibbs state reduces to a rank-2 spectral sum (explicit formula with e^{±βr} terms) enabling O(d_j) computation.
Empirical claim: typical equity covariance condition numbers κ(Σ) reported as in the range 10^3 to 10^5 for n ≈ 100–500 (Section 8.1).

Iteration complexity comparisons (informal table): IPM O(√r log(1/ε)) iterations with high precision; MW O(R^2 / ε^2) iterations with moderate precision; MW (quantum) O(√r / ε^2) iterations (presented as comparative figures).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper asserts theoretical quantum complexity improvements for MW-based SOCP solvers by exploiting rank-2 Lorentz-cone structure (informal complexity scaling like exponential-of-constant-times √r times polynomial factors), but these claims are presented at a theoretical level under strong data-access assumptions (coherent qRAM-like queries) and are not empirically demonstrated; the authors also note dequantization and input-model caveats that limit practical guarantees.
limitations: SOCP→SDP naive embedding loses structure and can increase computational cost (explicit).

Oracle structure requirement: the MW per-iteration O(N) savings rely on oracles returning arrowhead (Lorentz) certificates; if the oracle returns general SDP spectral certificates the complexity can degrade to O(N^3) per iteration (explicit).
Quantum speedups depend critically on strong data-access assumptions (qRAM / coherent query access); practical relevance is contingent on these input models (explicit).
Dequantized (quantum-inspired) classical algorithms require sample-and-query access; such access models may not hold for all finance datasets (explicit).

Conditioning sensitivity: poor scaling / large condition numbers (covariance matrices) inflate the MW width parameter and slow convergence; preprocessing (shrinkage, factor extraction, equilibration) is necessary (explicit).
Cardinality-constrained portfolio optimization is NP-hard; SDP relaxations may have nontrivial relaxation gaps and only provide bounds (explicit).
Numerical stability issues for Gibbs/arrowhead exponentials at low temperature (large βr); asymptotic and special-case handling required to avoid instability (explicit).
Learning-rate selection: the optimal MW learning rate requires knowledge of T (total iterations) in advance; mis-specification leads to instability or slow convergence (explicit).

MW methods are first-order and require many iterations to reach high precision compared to interior-point methods (IPM); MW is better suited to moderate-accuracy targets, not high-precision (explicit).
Per-iteration costs can be dominated by the oracle implementation (Coracle), e.g., O(mN) for sampling or matrix-vector products (explicit).
The paper's claims about quantum SOCP speedups are presented informally; rigorous end-to-end resource accounting (qubits, coherence, error rates) is not provided here (explicit).

contradictions: The paper itself qualifies quantum speedup claims by showing that classical 'dequantized' or sampling-based methods can match some of the putative quantum improvements under realistic sample-and-query access models, contradicting unconditional assertions of quantum superiority (i.e., quantum advantage depends heavily on data-access assumptions and conditioning).

Although the manuscript proves theoretical quantum-complexity improvements under coherent qRAM-style access, it also highlights conditioning and input-model caveats that limit practical scaling, tempering broad claims that quantum MW/SDP methods will straightforwardly scale to real-world portfolio sizes.
